To clarify the title for people: the labor participation rate (measured by (#employed)/(working population)) is as low as it's been since 1978. This is a bad thing.

I think the labor participation rate is the most important statistic in the economy. The unemployment rate has an arbitrary and easily manipulated denominator, excluding people who "aren't actively looking." Frankly I don't even know if I would be considered "actively seeking employment." What I do know is that I don't have a job, and if somebody offered, I'd work for them. But by BLS standards I don't know if I'm "unemployed". That ambiguity in the unemployment rate is a big problem.

Whereas the labor participation rate is much more all-encompassing, and a much larger sample, and thus paints a much clearer picture. It's also easier to see trends over time because it's a very simple number.

Wages are at such a shitty level that enough people have decided it's not worth the effort. If you're lucky enough to survive by other means, why go through the hassle of being constantly on call, having schedules that keep you out of every social gathering, being yelled at to constantly perform better, and getting no sick hours or any other form of compensation besides a paycheck that covers just a bit more than the cost of commuting?
there are some demographic realities that contribute to this but I agree it's a good economic indicator and consistent with what anyone paying attention to the world around them can observe.
